title: why are so many people remaking games that already exist?
author: MikeRadical
selftext:
I'm sorry if this comes off as a dig, i like making games with AI too so its not an anti AI thing. 

But I see a lot of "claude remade this old game/game that already exists - claude is amazing". And while yes its impressive, its also making something where it has a tonne of reference material. 

I see a lot of creative new games on here for sure - but I just don't get making a clone of something without adding to it/changing the game loop. 

Is this not a waste of your own time and tokens? 

Is it just to see if it can? 

I see this in vibe coding in general. I'm a musician and the subs I hang out on get the same vibe coded existing tools posted daily. Simple concepts that already exist in many forms.

I would get it if you really wanted it to have a new art style or look - but so many are happy with the default claude UI that we end up with an inferior version of a game from 20 years ago. 

That being said, the GTA clones always make me laugh.

comments.author: wewerecreaturres
comments.body: The most likely answer is that creating a new take on a successful product is a fully viable business model

replies.author: MikeRadical
replies.body:
Yeah that's a new take on something, which I've already said makes sense. We see that a lot in indie gaming in general. 

I'm talking about people more or less making an existing product. I saw one recently where the person made PLants vs zombies. That already exists.

replies.author: wewerecreaturres
replies.body: There will always be low effort attempts at everything

comments.author: nberthdev
comments.body:
I feel like AI prompting lends itself too well to copycats. Creativity requires real exploration and understanding of the underlying mechanics, both in terms of game design and in terms of engineering, and many people using AI for one-shot games just haven't done that work. So the best they can do is think in terms of "re-make this". 

Which, to be fair, is how a lot of people always have thought, except that when you're not just prompting the AI you had to learn how to do it yourself, and through trial and error came upon happy little mistakes...

That's my take anyway.

comments.author: tightsweatpants
comments.body:
Many people have said this but most games are remakes of other games. Castlevania is just Metroid with different mechanics, music, and in-game power ups. Every JRPG is essentially the same.

Art direction, composition, creative use of dialogue and storytelling, and ultimately execution of the feeling you want your game to give people is key.

Spitting out random reskins is not good execution.

comments.author: DigitalDustChan
comments.body: AI requires a lot more direction when you make something new than it does when you ask it to remake something it already knows.

replies.author: MikeRadical
replies.body:
I understand it's a lot easier but that doesn't make it any less useless/uninteresting/redundant. Like what is the person gaining from prompting "hey Claude, copy this" 

Like what is compelling somebody to spend time and money on something that already exists and had an established fan base.

replies.author: SandshrewPoke
replies.body: Some ppl use it as a benchmark

replies.author: DigitalDustChan
replies.body:
\> what is compelling somebody to spend time and money on something that already exists and had an established fan base.

It's the same compelling reason that Google, Amazon, Uber, Airbnb, etc was built on. Copying and iterating is 95% of all business and art.

replies.author: MikeRadical
replies.body:
Everybody's example includes a step that I am not talking about. Iterating, building upon, reimagining. 

I feel like so much of Reddit has people so desperate to be heard but nobody stops to read the question.

Google removed all information overload and made a simple single page website. Uber invented ridesharing and Airbnb was a UX idea that turned into a new business model. 

What did you mean by these examples?

replies.author: DigitalDustChan
replies.body: Google took search engines and copied them. Uber took taxies and copied them. Airbnb took craigslist and copied it

replies.author: MikeRadical
replies.body:
Google improved upon the search engine with a better UX model. Uber invented ride sharing. Airbnb created a new market and business model. 

None of these are video games.

LOL cause an LLM can only reproduce things which it has tons of examples of in it's pre training data. 

I wonder how many tokens thousands of people have chewed up making minecraft clones? 

If you were trying to create something very unique, you would have a very long set of prompts back and forth with 100s of prompts and iterations.  

You can prompt "make me snake game" in single prompt. 

You can't prompt something unique in a few prompts though.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
Three theories then, based on your edit.

Quick and dirty cash grabs. I built a clone of cookie clicker, changed the theme and threw it on itch within a week. It just shows that if you are happy to copy then you can get to market quickly and take your chances.

AI has unlocked a whole load of people who could never have built anything before and they are just really excited they’ve built a game. Coding was a huge barrier. Art is becoming less of a challenge. Game design and originality is the AI weak spot. Therefore you get asset swaps and clones of existing games with proud owners happy to share.

Outside bet… the one shot amazing game posts are actually AI company marketing.

comments.author: Due_Answer_4230
comments.body:
Because it really is easier to make things that you’ve already been shown. AI know how to do these things because they’ve seen pieces or the whole thing plenty of times. So we see these posted on socials. 

Going outside the known distribution and doing something new is hard. AI struggle, you need to be more involved. Polish is hard. Both art and engineering are harder. So it takes time and there are more failures - these do not get posted to socials.

comments.author: 0bscuris
comments.body:
I know for me, there is alot of games from the late 90’s early 2000’s like: gangsters organized crime, sacrifice, sim ant and others where the concepts and mechanics were really cool but just not really there yet.

Those products are too niche for a large studio to take them on. If you do another madden game, or fps, nobody is going to get fired cuz the decision isn’t risky.

If u bet on an innovative weird idea snd it fails, ur losing ur job.

But now with ai, the size of the customer base is irrelevant because the inputs r really cheap and so the product can be as niche as it wants.

comments.author: CubersumGame
comments.body:
Back before the advent of AI, these people expressed themselves differently - in real life they would deck themselves out in heavy gold chains, while online they spent real money on the most expensive in-game items.

Now, they are making "oneshot copy".

I’ve seen interesting oneshots that didn't exist before - and in those cases, the situation is understandable: the person didn't have the chance to learn how to draw or code, yet they had an idea. But a copy of an existing game is pure emptiness; it means the person has absolutely nothing inside.

It’s all just a way to buy attention for a person who amounts to nothing.
